title: Mohnish Pabrai's Session with Columbia Business School (CSIMA) on February 14, 2024
summary: Pabrai opens with the observation that Buffett's 12 needle-moving decisions in 58 years imply a 3-4% hit rate, and argues that one great idea every five years is almost a law of value investing because differentiated views require months-long 'rabbit holes' (BNSF, See's, Coke). He describes his own evolution from great businesses to hardcore Graham in 2000 and back again (five years late), Berkshire after Munger, being a harsh grader that rejects most ideas in 60 seconds, his current rabbit holes in car dealerships and coal (Consol, met coal), and holding around ten concentrated bets for decades.

ideas.idea: Buffett's 12 needle-moving decisions over 58 years, out of an estimated 300-400 important ones, imply a 3-4% hit rate, and one great idea every five years may be almost a law of value investing.
ideas.detail: Outsized returns require a differentiated view from the market; such views are either delusional (Buffett probably had one or two dozen of those) or correct, and getting to conviction takes deep, slow work.

ideas.idea: Buffett and Munger's record would be a shadow of itself if they hadn't been learning machines; BNSF required destroying their best-loved idea that railroads are stupid.
ideas.detail: Rebuilt bridges allowing double-stack cars and efficiency gains tipped rail over trucks for long haul; both admitted being late, with Cascade Investments (Gates' money) and possibly Bill Ackman figuring it out years earlier.

ideas.idea: A deep dive takes about three months, so you get roughly 20 per five years and 100-150 in a lifetime out of 50,000 possible rabbit holes; many are dry wells, and you only need to get rich once.
ideas.detail: If one in three that look great turns out great, 20 dives might yield three or four interesting ideas and one good one. Anomalies aren't handed to you on a platter; you must choose which rabbit holes to enter and make some of them count.

ideas.idea: See's Candies taught Buffett about pricing power and brands, a learning that took two decades to turn into the Coke investment and 40-50 years to turn into Apple.
ideas.detail: Every January 1 Buffett raised See's prices at roughly twice inflation (10-15%) with no volume pushback; volumes grew under 2% a year versus ~4% California GDP growth from 1970-90. He couldn't have bought Coke in 1975, 1980 or 1985.

ideas.idea: Insurance was a terrible business for Berkshire for 20 years; what you are looking for are anomalies like Ajit Jain and GEICO showing up.
ideas.detail: From the mid-1960s to mid-1980s insurance didn't work for Berkshire; there is no successor for Ajit and that business would shrink when he leaves.

ideas.idea: His philosophy went Munger, Graham, Munger: great businesses in the 1990s, hardcore Graham after the 1999-2000 bubble, and back to great businesses starting around 2018, five or six years late.
ideas.detail: In March 2000 Microsoft was $600B on single-digit-billion cash flows (~70x) and flatlined until 2012, while Berkshire fell from 70,000 to 40,000 as people sold it to buy dot-coms; he bought funeral homes at 2x and steel mills at 3x earnings. He should have switched back in 2012-13 when great businesses' valuations had come into line, and would write The Dhandho Investor differently now.

ideas.idea: Berkshire is as close to bulletproof as you can get post-Munger because its culture and written record are so deeply entrenched, though size will eventually force dividends or heavy buybacks.
ideas.detail: Buffett says Berkshire was built to Munger's blueprint with Buffett as general contractor; without Munger it wouldn't be 5-10% of its current market cap. Munger, a type-A dictator elsewhere, said it was very smart of him to be Buffett's junior partner; he pushed Buffett to go big on Costco and Buffett bought Gen Re without consulting him.

ideas.idea: Be a harsh grader: reject most companies in 60 seconds or less, give survivors 5-10 minutes, then an hour, then a day or two; most ideas should die at each stage.
ideas.detail: Whole sections of Value Line like biotech and pharma are discarded outright. Passing on Google or Microsoft ten years ago as too rich was probably a mistake but not the end of the world because more pitches keep coming.

ideas.idea: Publicly traded car dealerships at mid-single-digit multiples are a current rabbit hole because the market's EV thesis (no parts and service, direct sales) looks wrong to him.
ideas.detail: Dealers make only 4-5% of profits on new cars but ~40% on parts and service; EVs have four or five battery modules costing ~$7,000 each to replace after ~10 years and $20-25k for a full pack at 13-14 years, plus brakes and tires, and OEMs going direct may cost more than the 3-4% dealer margin.

ideas.idea: The moment data tells you your thesis is completely wrong, you're done; red flags can come from anywhere.
ideas.detail: Given as the answer to when to stop digging, using the dealership thesis as the example of testing each pillar.

ideas.idea: There is always a bear market somewhere; the edge today is qualitative thinking that finds an aha moment, not more data, and broadening to other geographies reveals wide price-value gaps.
ideas.detail: The Dow was 400 in the 1930s and still 400 in 1954, breeding a generation that thought stocks were no place to make money, which set up great returns in the 1950s-60s and after 1973-74. Munger lamented nothing was buyable, yet car dealers trade at mid-single-digit multiples and Delta and the top four airlines with airport oligopolies may be worth a look.

ideas.idea: Metallurgical coal will be mined for at least five to seven more decades because there is no practical alternative for making steel; new blast furnaces commissioned in the 2030s have 50-year lives.
ideas.detail: He spent about seven months in the coal rabbit hole and 11 days in four large US mines, going 2,000 feet underground; he steers students toward met coal over thermal and says his latest 13F holds nothing but coal.

ideas.idea: IPSCO (2003-04) was the template: $15 cash per share, $15 a share of contracted cash flow for two years, stock at $40, so he took a 10% position just to see how Mr. Market priced $45 of cash in 24 months.
ideas.detail: A year later it guided another $15, the stock reached $80-90, and at 14-15 months a Swedish company bid $160; he sold at 152 within seconds. At 2-3x earnings ex-cash, management should have bought back every share, but managers are a brick wall on buybacks.

ideas.idea: Consol Energy is a coupon-clipping IPSCO bet: it forward-sells production at locked prices (half of 2024, half of 2025, ~40% of 2026 sold in 2023), coal is a four-letter word no endowment will touch, and it was already buying back stock.
ideas.detail: The aha came from a Twitter post in May 2023 comparing David Einhorn's Consol bet to IPSCO; Consol was Einhorn's largest 13F position aside from Green Brick. Pabrai urged them to drop the dividend for all buybacks, which they announced the next quarter; investing is opportunistic with no strategy, you go where your nose takes you.

ideas.idea: Be an inch wide and a mile deep, starting with products and services you use and love, because any business that extracts a dollar from a discerning consumer must be spectacular.
ideas.detail: Apple's rabbit hole no longer has much meat on the bone; read everything in sight including Value Investors Club write-ups and be the shameless cloner.

ideas.idea: Concentration isn't a real problem: 10 million US entrepreneurs are 95-98% all in on one business and sleep fine, while he has never gone 100% and usually holds ten bets.
ideas.detail: The first-generation Chinese couple opening a restaurant in Queens has all their money and time in it; even a concentrated portfolio still has four or five bets.

ideas.idea: The ideal is to find a great rabbit hole and do nothing for 10-20 years; returns may take years to show up and then keep coming for two or three decades, if your capital base allows it.
ideas.detail: Timeframe depends on whether it's your money or an investor base that lets you play your hand out.

ideas.idea: Start investing on your own as early as possible for a long runway; you can learn from the giants at a distance like Ekalavya rather than needing a formal apprenticeship.
ideas.detail: The documented body of work of great investors makes it relatively easy to learn remotely if you are serious.
